486-ozma-of-oz-a-record-of-her-adventure:
L. Frank Baum brings Dorothy back to Oz in this tale, after a storm casts her ashore in the land of Ev. With Billina the yellow hen, Tik-Tok the machine man, and old friends, she faces Princess Langwidere's many heads and the Nome King, who holds Ev's royal family as ornaments. Eleven guesses decide their fate.

Baum writes with wit and warmth, letting Billina's sharp tongue save the day. The Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, and Cowardly Lion join the rescue. The book charms as a bright sequel, where courage, craft, and a hen's nerve beat a king's greed.
doe-osti-3016989-experiences-with-sycl-o: SYCL got AMD-GPU-experienced, and this DOE text runs Kokkos on the hardware. The pages detail the findings. The computing folks get their data. The GPUs were AMD. The data were computing. The hardware was Kokkos. The experiences were SYCL.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WinterKillsByRi: nsia-WinterKillsByRichardCondon Winter Kills By Richard Condon: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-slavic-aryan-vedas-a: Aleksandr Khinevich's Slavic-Aryan Vedas presents texts such as the Santiya Veda of Perun and the Haratya as ancient Slavic scripture. Mainstream scholars do not accept these works as old sources. The library holds the volume as an archive item, without backing, and classes it as fringe material. It serves the study of modern mythmaking: new scriptures written for movements that want a very old past.
ozma-of-oz-a-record-of-her-adventures-wi:
L. Frank Baum's Ozma of Oz is the third Oz book. It records Princess Ozma's adventures with Dorothy Gale of Kansas. The long title delights in listing the company. The Yellow Hen, the Scarecrow, and the Tin Woodman come. Tiktok, the Cowardly Lion, and the Hungry Tiger follow. The contents run from The Girl in the Chicken Coop through the heads of Langwidere and the Nome King to Dorothy's magic belt.

In his author's note Baum credits the children. Their letters plead to know more about Dorothy, ask what became of the Cowardly Lion and what Ozma did after becoming ruler of Oz, and even suggest plots. This volume answers them, taking Dorothy by storm and shipwreck out of Kansas and into the land of Ev.
podcast-joerogan-jNOQadUbo-k:
Comedian James McCann joins Joe Rogan for episode 2488. McCann is an Australian comic who built a name with sharp, odd sets. Rogan's stage has become a rite for rising comics.

The v1 note for the episode stays spare, so the guest carries the hour. McCann trades stories of clubs, hecklers, and the road. Rogan tests his takes on America and its habits. The talk flows as a classic Rogan hang: long, loose, and funny. New listeners meet a fresh voice on the biggest platform comedy has. A spare record leaves his act to speak.
podcast-joerogan-xz7jtzGsa-k:
Researcher Jacques Vallee and filmmaker James Fox join Joe Rogan together in episode 1574 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Fox directed The Phenomenon and other well-known UFO films. Vallee brings decades of case research, giving the pair a scientist-and-storyteller balance.

Fox shares what he learned filming witnesses, officials, and crash-site claims around the world. Vallee adds the patterns he sees across thousands of reports and warns against easy answers. Rogan guides them through famous cases old and new. Serious listeners get two of the field's best-known voices in one long conversation.
podcast-joerogan-yWrfEclkC_k:
America's opioid crisis, and the drug industry's share of blame, is the subject of this Joe Rogan Experience segment. Millions became addicted after pain pills were sold as safe and pushed hard by makers and marketers. Rogan and his guest tell the story plain, as an American tragedy.

They trace how aggressive sales, friendly doctors, and weak oversight flooded towns with pills. The talk covers the human cost in overdoses and broken families that followed. Questions of profit and punishment run through the whole account. For the grieving and the angry alike, it lays out how the pills, the profits, and the bodies connect.
representative-plays-by-american-dramati:
Paul Kauvar; or, Anarchy represents Steele Mackaye in this set of American plays, with an essay weighing his place in the theatre. Mackaye lived from 1844 to 1894. The essay grants his play a serious social purpose, yet finds the old romantic form too weak to carry such matter well.

Mackaye's strength lay in vigour: large scenes, mob movement, and a big brush, as critic Nym Crinkle put it. He built a double stage for the little Madison Square playhouse, a first step toward later stage machines. Trained under Delsarte, he preached natural acting, and once held Longfellow, Bryant, and Edwin Booth spellbound for two hours at the Lotos Club.
the-forest-runners-a-story-of-the-great-:
Joseph A. Altsheler wrote The Forest Runners as a tale of the great war trail in early Kentucky, first printed in 1908. It stands in his Young Trailers series with The Young Trailers and The Keepers of the Trail.

The front pages list Altsheler's many sets: French and Indian War tales, Texan tales, Civil War tales, and Great West tales. His boys' books mix scouting, hunting, and war paths with close woodcraft. In this tale young runners cross a Kentucky thick with foes, where a dropped sign or a snapped twig can cost a life, and speed and silence are a boy's best arms.
the-young-engineers-in-arizona-or-laying:
H. Irving Hancock opens The Young Engineers in Arizona in Abe Morris's barber shop. Two customers bet on flies sitting on their mirrors. The wager jumps from ten dollars to twenty. Each man sits tucked in white, mid-haircut, watching his fly. The bet's maker is Jim Duff, a notorious local gambler. Hancock calls him among the meanest Arizona ever hosted.

Traditions about honest gamblers, the narrator scoffs, fool only newcomers. Tom Reade and Harry Hazelton, the young engineers, will face such men. Their job lays railroad tracks across dangerous quicksand. The subtitle calls it the man-killer quicksand. Boys' adventure readers get gambling, grit, and engineering hazards combined.
